blocks.text: Summarization fine-tuning trains a model to compress a longer document into a shorter version that preserves the important content, one of the narrower, well defined generation tasks covered in this module, in contrast to the open-ended text generation covered in an earlier topic.

This topic covers the extractive versus abstractive distinction, how to structure training data, and the practical challenges around document length and hallucination that are specific to summarization.

Summarization fine-tuning teaches a model to take a longer input document and produce a shorter output that preserves its key content, a well defined transformation task compared to the more open-ended text generation covered in an earlier topic.

Extractive summarization selects and stitches together existing sentences directly from the source document, abstractive summarization generates entirely new sentences that convey the same meaning, modern fine-tuned language models are typically used for abstractive summarization, since they can produce more fluent, concise output than sentence selection alone allows.

blocks.text: Training data pairs a source document with a human written reference summary, the more closely the reference summaries match the length, tone, and level of detail actually wanted in production, the better the fine-tuned model will match that same target behavior.

blocks.text: 4. Handling Documents That Exceed Context Length

blocks.alt: Handling Documents That Exceed Context Length

blocks.text: Some source documents exceed a model context window, covered in an earlier module, requiring either chunking the document and summarizing each piece before a final combining pass, or using a model variant specifically capable of longer context, a genuinely different challenge than summarizing documents that comfortably fit in context.

ROUGE, covered in an earlier topic, is the traditional metric for tracking summarization content coverage during training, but hallucination evaluation, also covered in an earlier topic, matters specifically here too, since a fluent summary that misstates a fact from the source document is a common and serious failure mode, human review remains valuable for catching both issues together.

blocks.title: Summarization has a uniquely high hallucination risk
blocks.content: Because summarization compresses information, a model can easily blend or misattribute details from different parts of a source document, producing a summary that reads well but subtly misrepresents what the source actually said.

blocks.text: A model fine-tuned on general news article summarization may not transfer well to a specialized domain, legal documents or medical records, where the important content to preserve looks quite different, domain-specific fine-tuning data usually produces noticeably better summaries for that domain than a general purpose model.

Including varied length instructions directly in training data, teaching the model to respond to explicit length requests, gives production flexibility that a model trained only on a single fixed summary length would not have.

Compared to the generic text generation fine-tuning covered in an earlier topic, summarization has a much more constrained, checkable notion of correctness, a good summary needs to actually reflect the source document content, not just be fluent and on-brand, this changes both how training data is built and how quality gets evaluated.

Summarization fine-tuning commonly supports document digest tools, meeting transcript summarization, and customer support ticket triage, cases where reading the full source text for every item is impractical and a fast, reliable summary provides real value.

A team building a meeting summary tool fine-tunes a model on transcript and human written summary pairs specific to their meeting format, including examples with explicit length instructions to give users control over summary detail.

During evaluation, they track ROUGE alongside a dedicated hallucination check comparing summary claims against the transcript, catching a pattern where the model occasionally attributed a statement to the wrong speaker, a hallucination class ROUGE alone would not have surfaced, prompting a targeted data fix.

items: Relying only on ROUGE and skipping a dedicated hallucination check for summarization specifically
Training on generic summaries when the production use case actually needs a specific domain focus
Not handling documents that exceed the model context length, producing truncated or incomplete summaries
Training on only one fixed summary length, losing the flexibility explicit length control would provide

blocks.text: Take a short article or document, write two summaries of it, one extractive by selecting key sentences directly and one abstractive by rephrasing in new sentences, and compare which one reads more naturally while still preserving the key content.

Summarization fine-tuning trains a model to abstractively compress documents into shorter summaries using document and reference summary training pairs, requiring both ROUGE tracking and dedicated hallucination checking to catch fluent but factually inaccurate output, a well defined transformation task distinct from the open-ended generic text generation covered earlier in this module.
